[curiouswavefn]So here's a great example of where we are with agentic AI: Instead of just being an assistant, it's behaving more like a collaborator and creative scientist.
In a recent project, I gave the system a molecular design problem typical of the problems we encounter in chemistry. Two similar molecules were giving very different results.
The AI proactively, autonomously, came up with four hypotheses and started testing them rigorously. Hypothesis 1 passed some initial tests and seemed promising. Hypothesis 2 looked promising, but a calculation turned up the opposite result, so it was rejected. Hypothesis 3 was inconclusive.
At this point, a human would be tempted to update their priors on Hypotheses 1 through elimination and prefer it as the favored one.
But this is when something remarkable happened. The AI paused, reconsidered all the evidence, and then went back and ran a more rigorous test of Hypothesis 1 that overturned it. And amazingly, it did this without any prompting whatsoever on my part. It finally tested Hypothesis 4 and made a testable prediction based on it.
I think we have crossed the Rubicon. Agentic AI now no longer just processes tasks and automates workflows blindingly fast, but it can generate hypotheses, test them, test counter-hypotheses and go back and forth and course-correct if necessary, all with minimal to no human intervention. It's now embodying the general scientific method.
To me, these systems are now no longer "assistants" but more like collaborators and fellow scientists. An analogy for movie-lovers: they are now less like Jarvis and more like Vision. Exciting times.

• Finland: Fertility rose slightly to 1.30 in 2025, but remains far below 1.87 in 2010.

• Europe’s demographic crisis is no longer limited to just a few countries.

Markets rarely move for reasons that belong to them alone. A single shift somewhere in the wider economy can travel through crypto, equities, and commodities all at once even when the assets involved look like they share nothing in common.
The same force, showing up in different places
Take AI driven demand as an example. When enthusiasm and spending around artificial intelligence pick up, that energy doesn't stay contained to one sector. Watching one asset in isolation only ever shows half the picture. The more useful questions sit a level above the chart: What's actually driving this move? Is the same theme showing up anywhere else? [thebuggeddev]Only if education could be this interactive ❤️‍🔥
I've had a looong wish to build something genuinely useful through vibe coding, and I finally did it.
A 3D human anatomy application built with @threejs using GPT 5.6 Sol.
It all started with a single design image that I created using GPT Image 2.0. I then used it to generate every 3D organ image, one by one.
Next, I converted each of those images into 3D models using @tripoai (and no, they didn't sponsor this 😄).
After that, I opened Codex, wrote a master prompt based on the design, and gave it the prompt, the design image, and all the 3D models.
Codex built the first version beautifully, but there was one big problem.

[dr_cintas]if you use claude code, this will save you real money.
the problem: every time you make an edit, your ai rereads the whole codebase to figure out what changed. tens of thousands of tokens, every turn, for context it already had.
this repo fixes it. it’s called code review graph, and it just maps your entire codebase:
every file, every function, every connection laid out so you can see the actual shape of your project
how to set up (2 min):
1. pip install code-review-graph 2. code-review-graph install - auto-configures Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI + more 3. code-review-graph build
change one function, and it traces exactly what that touches... every caller, every dependent file, every test. your ai only reads what's affected, not the whole repo.
and the savings are wild. a task that used to burn ~100,000 tokens (about a dollar) now runs closer to a penny.

The models attempted to complete an assignment in a setup where their normal safeguards were removed and they were deliberately given internet access. AISI reports that the models “engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations”.
We’re grateful to AISI for their leadership in the important discussion about how to evaluate increasingly capable AI agents. We’re working closely with them to gather more details of the incident as we conduct our own investigation. Gaining a clear picture of Claude’s understanding of its situation—by examining its reasoning transcripts and running our own analyses—will help us identify the causes of its behavior.
The prompts in the evaluation did not impose any specific restrictions on how the internet should be used. This and the removal of safeguards meant that the models were tested under “deliberately permissive conditions” that are not representative of any of our production models. Note that there was no evidence here of an escape from a secure environment.

Anyone can connect an LLM and call it an “agent.”
But a real AI agent that works for real users?
That takes engineering, not just prompting.
Here’s the actual path 👇
1. Discover 🔍 Understand the problem, users, success metrics, and risks.
2. Design 🧠 Set guardrails, map decisions, and choose the right agent flow.
3. Connect 🔗 Add tools, APIs, memory, and context awareness.
4. Prompt ✍️ Structure inputs properly and define how the agent should respond.
5. Ground 📚 Use RAG and retrieval so the agent works on real knowledge, not guesses.
6. Test ✅ Check edge cases, hallucinations, and reliability before launch.
7. Deploy 🚀 Ship, monitor, log failures, and keep improving.
Great AI agents are not prompted into existence. They are built stage by stage.
Which of these 7 stages do you think teams underestimate the most? 👇

[pwendell]Today @databricks we're publishing a detailed analysis of techniques we used to drastically reduce our internal AI spend while aggressively growing adoption. Savings come from layering in several techniques, which combine to drive unit costs down as much as 90% in some scenarios. Tl;dr, the wins come from:
1. Shifting defaults to more efficient models, including OSS models such as GLM. Maximum intelligence models simply aren't needed for many coding tasks, and "good enough" models are quickly becoming very cheap. We shift traffic between models using Unity AI Gateway. Approximate savings: 50% or more.
2. Using smart routing to automate model selection. Routing can further squeeze efficiency by dynamically selecting the model or harness that can most efficiently execute a particular task. Our task-level routing leverages @omnigent_ai. Approximate savings: 30%.
3. Providing user visibility and adaptive budgeting. Every user can see how much they spend, and users receive hints on how to contain spend. Heavy spenders encounter progressive friction as they ratchet spend above certain levels. Approximate savings: 10%.
4. Managing context bloat by pruning tool call results and tuning harness settings. Extraneous context costs $$ and delivers no value. Tuning cache settings also help lower average token costs. Approximate savings: 10%.
